title: Act II, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: Artemidorus, a teacher of rhetoric, reads aloud a letter he has written naming the conspirators and warning Caesar to look about him. He plans to stand in the street and hand it to Caesar on the way to the Capitol, lamenting that virtue cannot live out of reach of envy.

context.history: This very short scene (Act II, Scene III) builds suspense just before the assassination. Plutarch reports that a man named Artemidorus tried to warn Caesar.

significance: The warnings multiply as the moment nears, so the assassination feels both preventable and inevitable.
discussionQuestions: Why do stories often add near-misses just before a disaster?
Where does structure appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with honor and self-deception?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act II, Scene III,” how does Shakespeare show Artemidorus's letter? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the structure you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act II, Scene III, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Artemidorus's letter? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the structure in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act II, Scene III develops the idea of Artemidorus's letter. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of structure and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act II, Scene III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its structure shape the reader's understanding of Artemidorus's letter. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act II, Scene III suggests about Artemidorus's letter. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's structure and tone / mood), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses structure in Act II, Scene III to complicate the reader's understanding of Artemidorus's letter. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act II, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Artemidorus's letter responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act II, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Artemidorus's letter follows or bends those conventions, using the structure as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act II, Scene III and its treatment of Artemidorus's letter. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's structure and tone / mood, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act II, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about Artemidorus's letter in Julius Caesar. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act II, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Artemidorus's letter. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Julius Caesar.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
